strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated gap: existing 'EEG tokenizers' (e.g., LaBraM, BIOT) are either continuous or only used during pretraining rather than as true discrete tokenizers at inference time; the paper proposes a genuinely discrete VQ-based tokenization pipeline used throughout training and inference.

The joint frequency-temporal design (Localized Spectral Window Encoder + Temporal Encoder + Temporal Transformer with frequency-band/temporal masking) is well grounded in the frequency representation collapse literature and is empirically validated via spectral entropy analysis showing richer frequency capture than a temporal-only encoder.

Broad and consistent empirical validation across four diverse EEG datasets/tasks (TUEV, TUAB, CHB-MIT, IIIC) with the proposed method outperforming strong, properly reproduced baselines (BIOT, LaBraM, and others) while using substantially fewer parameters.

Thorough ablation studies (raw-only vs STFT-only vs joint, masking strategy, presence/absence of positional encoding, vocabulary size, effect of masked-token-prediction pretraining) that support the design choices and add credibility to the claims.

Novel and thoughtful token-quality analysis (token utilization, class-token uniqueness score, similar-class retrieval via Jaccard similarity, spectral entropy) that goes beyond typical performance tables and provides some interpretability evidence.
Demonstrated plug-and-play benefit: replacing LaBraM's neural tokenizer with TFM-Tokenizer improves LaBraM's own downstream performance, supporting the claim of a reusable, scalable tokenizer.
Qualitative visualization of learned tokens (Figure 5) showing recognizable, class-consistent EEG motifs (e.g., token 4035 in PLED), supporting interpretability claims.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains, while consistent, are often modest (e.g., TUEV balanced accuracy 0.468→0.494) and standard deviations are sometimes large relative to the improvement (e.g., ±0.05 on TUEV balanced accuracy), so some comparisons may not be statistically robust; no significance testing is reported despite 5-seed runs.

The paper's central architectural motivation of avoiding cross-channel dependencies is somewhat in tension with the fact that many downstream tasks (e.g., seizure detection, multi-class event classification) inherently benefit from spatial/cross-channel information; the TFM-Encoder still aggregates multi-channel tokens for classification, so the single-channel tokenizer claim is not as clean a departure from prior work as suggested, and no controlled experiment isolates the benefit of avoiding cross-channel tokenization versus other architectural changes (e.g., linear attention, discretization itself).

All experiments are conducted in a single-dataset (train/test on same corpus) setting; despite the paper's framing around 'scalability across diverse EEG settings and channel configurations,' there is no cross-dataset or cross-channel-configuration transfer experiment (e.g., pretraining tokenizer on one dataset/montage and testing on another with different channels), which would be the most direct test of the claimed scalability.

The vocabulary-size ablation (Appendix A.4) shows no clear monotonic benefit for Cohen's Kappa or Weighted F1, which somewhat undercuts the narrative that larger, more expressive discrete vocabularies straightforwardly improve token quality.

The architecture is fairly complex (dual-path frequency/temporal encoders, gated aggregation, multiple transformers, extensive hyperparameter search via Ray Tune/Optuna across three phases), raising reproducibility concerns if code/checkpoints are not released; the paper does not mention public code availability.

The interpretability analysis, while interesting, is largely qualitative (a handful of visual examples) and the quantitative class-token uniqueness/retrieval metrics, though favorable, are still low in absolute terms (e.g., ~1-2% uniqueness, ~9-13% utilization), suggesting the tokens may still be far from a clean, disentangled, class-discriminative vocabulary.

Removing positional encoding is justified post-hoc via an ablation showing better numbers, but the explanation (EEG being 'chaotic and non-stationary') is somewhat hand-wavy and could benefit from deeper analysis given how central positional information usually is to sequence modeling.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: designing a reusable, data-driven EEG tokenizer (as opposed to LaBraM's tokenizer, which is discarded after pretraining and only used as a training objective).

Technically reasonable dual-path (time+frequency) architecture with a Localized Spectral Window Encoder and explicit time-frequency masked prediction objective, motivated by known issues (frequency entanglement/collapse) in time-series modeling.

Broad empirical evaluation across four standard EEG benchmarks (TUEV, TUAB, IIIC-Seizure, CHB-MIT) in both single- and multi-dataset pretraining settings, with consistent improvements over strong reproduced baselines (BIOT*, LaBraM*/†).
Demonstrates plug-and-play compatibility with existing foundation models (BIOT, LaBraM), showing the tokenizer can be swapped in to improve their performance, which supports the generalization claim.

Interesting scalability experiment on ear-EEG sleep staging, a genuinely out-of-distribution setting (different device, channel configuration, and task), showing the single-channel design has practical transferability.

Extensive ablations (masking strategy, vocabulary size, positional embeddings, number of downstream transformer layers, frequency vs. temporal-only variants) and token-quality analyses (class-token uniqueness, retrieval-based consistency, spectral entropy, utilization) that go beyond simple accuracy numbers and support interpretability claims.
Good reproducibility statement, detailed appendix with hyperparameters, dataset/preprocessing details, and code availability claim.
Achieves competitive/better performance with substantially fewer parameters than baselines (as small as 1.9M vs. LaBraM 5.8M/8.6M tokenizer), suggesting practical efficiency benefits.
weaknesses: Improvement claims are somewhat inconsistently presented: the abstract/intro highlight top-line gains (17%, 14%, 4%) that are cherry-picked from the best cases, while some appendix tables (e.g., Table 9) show mixed or even negative results on certain metrics (e.g., BIOT-TFM balanced accuracy drops from 0.4679 to 0.4228 on single-dataset TUEV, and BIOT-TFM balanced accuracy also drops on CHB-MIT), which somewhat undercuts the "consistently boosts performance" and "93% of cases improve" narrative in the main text/figures that selectively show only favorable metrics (Cohen's Kappa, AUC-PR).

The comparison to LaBraM is only fully fair after re-training LaBraM on the same restricted 4-dataset corpus (LaBraM†), since the original LaBraM used ~2500 hours of pretraining data; while this is disclosed, it somewhat limits the strength of claims about outperforming "foundation models" in their originally intended large-data regime.

Reported token utilization is quite low (roughly 6–14% of an 8192-size vocabulary is actually used), raising concerns about potential codebook underutilization/collapse that are only partially investigated (vocabulary-size ablation shows non-monotonic trends in Kappa/F1).

Some ear-EEG scalability results (Table 3) show relatively small absolute gains with overlapping/large standard deviations (e.g., balanced accuracy 0.4148 ± 0.0209 vs. 0.3890 ± 0.0182), so the claimed "14% outperformance" should be interpreted cautiously given the reported variance and the small labeled sample size (~8K).

Novelty of the dual-path time-frequency masking design is somewhat incremental relative to established ideas in general time-series representation learning (e.g., frequency-domain modeling, joint time-frequency masking used elsewhere), and the paper's claim of being "first" to encode time-frequency motifs as discrete tokens could be more carefully positioned against adjacent motif-learning and multi-domain tokenization literature outside EEG.

The qualitative motif analysis (Figure 5) is a small-scale, illustrative case study rather than a systematic clinical validation, so claims about physiological interpretability, while plausible, remain preliminary.

Statistical significance testing is reported only for a subset of comparisons (e.g., p-values mentioned for IIIC and ear-EEG but not consistently across all tables), making it harder to assess robustness of all claimed gains, especially given relatively high variance in several seizure-related metrics.
